summary: Describes a mechanism for basic IPv6 multihoming support at site exit routers, and its operational requirements.

plainLanguage.summary: It describes how a place with two exit roads can still keep its address working.

questions: how does multihoming work without growing the routing table
what are primary and secondary links in multihoming
how does ingress filtering affect multihoming
subtitle: How a site with two ISPs can survive a link failure without adding routes to the worldwide IPv6 routing table.

tldr.problem: A site connected to two ISPs wants to keep working when one link fails, but the usual IPv4 tricks add extra routes to the worldwide routing table, which does not fit IPv6 operational practice.
tldr.mechanism: The site takes a separate prefix from each ISP, then adds a backup (secondary) tunnel link from each ISP router to the other exit router, using strong and weak route preferences in BGP or RIPng so the primary link is used until it fails.
tldr.outcome: Inbound and outbound packets survive the failure of a link on either side, with no new protocol and no change to the global routing table. It does not pick the best exit or balance load.

facts.label: Tunnels, N ISPs all backing up

today: RFC 3178 is an Informational RFC and is not marked as obsoleted or updated in the unit metadata. It describes how to operate existing protocols, not a new one, and builds on RFC 2260.

sections.title: The Routing Table Problem
sections.content:
IPv6 addresses are 4 times wider than IPv4 addresses, so a bloated routing table would hurt router memory and lookup performance even more. The IPv6 addressing design therefore relies on aggregated announcements to keep the number of routes in the default-free zone small, and the 6bone guideline suggests that ASes do not announce non-aggregatable routes there.

IPv4 sites get better reachability by obtaining a portable prefix, or by announcing one ISP's prefix through several providers. Both techniques inject extra routes into the worldwide table, so they clash with IPv6 practice. This RFC offers a way to configure site exit routers and ISP routers that avoids that. It is largely based on RFC 2260.
sections.plainLanguage: If every house with two doors asked the whole town to redraw the map, the map would become huge. This idea lets houses have two doors without redrawing it.

sections.title: Goals and Non-Goals
sections.content:
The goal is better packet delivery between the site and the outside, in both directions, even when some of the site's exit links are down.

Three things are explicitly not goals: choosing the "best" exit link (the RFC notes there is no common definition of best), load-balancing between exit links, and coping with the breakage of any of the upstream ISPs.
sections.plainLanguage: The only promise is that you can still get out if one door is blocked. It does not promise the shortest path, and it does not share the traffic evenly.

sections.title: Primary and Secondary Links
sections.content:
The design follows RFC 2260 section 5.2. A site is connected to two ISPs, ISP-A and ISP-B, and receives a prefix from each: Pref-A and Pref-B. The site's exit routers are E-BR-A and E-BR-B, and the ISP routers are ISP-BR-A and ISP-BR-B. Inside the site, routes for both prefixes are exchanged so hosts can talk without using an external link.

Each exit router has a primary link to its own ISP router. A secondary link, usually an IP-over-IP tunnel, connects ISP-BR-A to E-BR-B and ISP-BR-B to E-BR-A. The secondary link should run over a different medium than the primary, so that one of them survives a link failure.

  • Inbound: E-BR-A announces Pref-A to ISP-BR-A with strong preference over the primary link, and Pref-B to ISP-BR-B with weak preference over the secondary link. E-BR-B does the mirror image.
  • Outbound: each ISP router announces a default route (or specific routes) toward its own exit router with strong preference, and toward the other exit router with weak preference.

Prefix A is always announced to ISP-BR-A and prefix B to ISP-BR-B. The weak routes sit in reserve as backup in both directions.
sections.plainLanguage: Each door has a main hallway and a hidden back passage to the other street. People use the main hallway, and only switch to the back passage if the main one is blocked.

sections.title: Applying It to IPv6, BGP4+ and RIPng
sections.content:
Because only Pref-A goes to ISP-BR-A and only Pref-B goes to ISP-BR-B, no extra announcements leave the site, which fits the 6bone aggregation guideline. No portable addresses are needed.

IPv6 lets a node hold several addresses, so a node can get an address from Pref-A, from Pref-B, or from both. When there are several, source address selection must happen when sending, but that is out of scope for this document. A simple approach is to put hosts on separate subnets, one per prefix.

The primary link can be native IPv6, an RFC 2893 IPv6-over-IPv4 tunnel, 6to4 (RFC 3056) or something else. If primary links are IPv6-over-IPv4 tunnels, the secondary link should also be IPv6-over-IPv4 rather than IPv6-over-IPv6, because the secondary link then has the same path MTU as the primary link.

With BGP4+, the RFC 2260 approach works as documented, and since the site is not doing transit it may not need a public AS number. With RIPng, routers raise the metric on the secondary link so the primary stays preferred; smaller metric means a stronger route.
sections.plainLanguage: In a computer network a machine can have more than one address, like a kid with a home address and a grandparent's address. The routers just make sure the main hallway looks shorter than the back passage.

sections.title: Trouble with Ingress Filters
sections.content:
If an upstream ISP applies ingress filters (RFC 2267) to outbound traffic, things get harder. A packet with a source in Pref-A must leave through ISP-BR-A, and one with a source in Pref-B through ISP-BR-B, but site routers do not route by source address, so a packet can easily reach the wrong border router.

One fix is to negotiate with both ISPs so that both prefixes are accepted as sources. That does not work if an ISP above ISP-A also filters, though the RFC says this should be rare because ingress filters are not suited to large ISPs with smaller ISPs beneath them.

Another fix is source-based routing at the exit routers with IPv6-over-IPv6 secondary tunnels. A packet from E-BR-A to ISP-BR-B carries an outer source in Pref-A (so it passes ISP-BR-A's filter) and an inner source in Pref-B (so it passes ISP-BR-B's filter after decapsulation). Not every router implements source-based routing, and its interaction with normal routing and filter rules varies by implementation.
sections.plainLanguage: Some guards only let you through a door if your address label matches that street. Wrapping your letter inside another envelope with the right label gets it past the first guard.

sections.title: Scaling, Failover and Experience
sections.content:
With many ISPs, making every pair back each other up needs O(N^2) tunnels. It is better to form N/2 pairs of ISPs that back each other up, choosing pairs unlikely to fail together, which needs only O(N) tunnels. For very large sites with links in far-apart places, such as the United States and Japan, use the technique only among nearby links, since a secondary link across the world adds excessive delay.

If a primary link stays down for a long time, an administrator can send router advertisements with the preferred lifetime of the unwanted prefix set to 0, so hosts treat those addresses as deprecated and stop using them as sources for new connections. The author does not recommend automating this with router renumbering, which could make the site unstable if links flap.

The co-author ran the setup with two upstream ISPs, four RFC 2893 tunnels in total and BGP4+ peering. Failover happened within the BGP hold time. It was tested with keepalive and hold times from 3 and 10 seconds up to 60 and 180 seconds.
sections.plainLanguage: If you have lots of doors, you only pair up nearby ones as backups. And if one street stays blocked for ages, you tell everyone to stop giving out that street's address.
